summary.text: An abelian group is a group in which the result of the operation on two elements does not depend on the order in which they are written.
The integers and the real numbers under addition are abelian groups, and the idea underlies fields, rings, vector spaces and algebras.
The concepts of abelian group and ℤ-module agree: every abelian group is a module over the ring of integers ℤ in a unique way.

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: The Norwegian mathematician Niels Henrik Abel

facts.label: Notation
facts.value: Additive notation is the usual one for modules and rings

facts.label: Cayley table test
facts.value: A finite group is abelian if its table is symmetric about the diagonal

facts.label: Every ring
facts.value: It is an abelian group under its addition

facts.label: Finite ones
facts.value: They are very well understood and fully classified

items.prompt: You write out the multiplication table of a finite group, with each product in the row and column of its two factors. How do you tell whether the group is abelian?

options.label: Every row repeats the same entries
The first row equals the first column only
The table has the identity on the diagonal
The table is symmetric about the main diagonal

items.explain: The group is abelian if and only if the table is symmetric about the main diagonal, since that says each product equals the product in the other order.

items.prompt: Matrix multiplication is generally not commutative. Which matrices still form an abelian group under multiplication?

options.label: The 2 × 2 rotation matrices
All invertible matrices
All square matrices of any size
All matrices with a zero entry

items.explain: Matrices, even invertible ones, do not generally form an abelian group, but some groups of matrices do, such as the 2 × 2 rotation matrices.

items.prompt: You take any ring and ignore its multiplication, keeping only addition. What structure is left?

options.label: A field
A non-abelian group
An abelian group
A vector space

items.explain: Every ring is an abelian group with respect to its addition operation.

items.prompt: You pick a subgroup of an abelian group and want to form a quotient group from it. Which subgroups allow this?

options.label: Only the trivial subgroup
Only the subgroups containing the identity alone
Only cyclic subgroups
Every subgroup

items.explain: Every subgroup of an abelian group is normal, so each subgroup gives rise to a quotient group.

items.prompt: In an abelian group written additively, you define nx as x + x + ⋯ + x (n summands). What structure does this give the group?

options.label: A module over the ring of integers ℤ
A field
A ring with identity
A module over the real numbers

items.explain: Defining nx this way makes the group a module over the ring ℤ of integers, and the modules over ℤ can be identified with abelian groups.

items.prompt: A finitely generated abelian group is taken apart into the simplest possible pieces. What two kinds of piece does it split into?

options.label: A cyclic part and a non-abelian part
A torsion group and a free abelian group
A field and a ring
A finite part and an infinite non-abelian part

items.explain: For finitely generated abelian groups, the structure theorem says the group splits as a direct sum of a torsion group and a free abelian group.

paragraphs.heading: Order does not matter
paragraphs.text: An abelian group, also known as a commutative group, is a group where combining two elements gives the same answer whichever one you write first. Put another way, its operation is commutative. A group whose operation fails this test is called non-abelian, or non-commutative. Camille Jordan chose the name to honour Niels Henrik Abel, a mathematician from Norway, who had found that when the group of a polynomial is commutative, the roots of that polynomial can be calculated using radicals.

paragraphs.heading: The other rules
paragraphs.text: Commutativity sits on top of the usual group rules. Grouping does not matter, so (a⋅b)⋅c always equals a⋅(b⋅c). There is an identity element e that leaves everything alone: e⋅a = a⋅e = a. And each element a has a partner b that brings it back to the identity, with a⋅b = b⋅a = e.

paragraphs.heading: Familiar examples
paragraphs.text: The integers under addition are the model case. Adding two integers gives another integer, addition is associative, zero is the identity, each n has the inverse −n, and n + m = m + n. The real numbers under addition form one too, and so do the nonzero reals under multiplication. Every cyclic group is abelian, which covers the integers modulo n, written ℤ/nℤ. Even the group holding nothing but its identity element counts.

paragraphs.heading: Where it fails
paragraphs.text: Matrices show how the rule can break. Multiplying two matrices usually gives a different result in the other order, so matrices, even invertible ones, generally fail to be an abelian group under multiplication. Some special collections do pass, though: the 2 × 2 rotation matrices form an abelian group under matrix multiplication.

paragraphs.heading: A test with a table
paragraphs.text: For a finite group there is a quick check. Build its Cayley table, a grid set up the way a multiplication table is. The group is abelian exactly when the grid mirrors itself across its main diagonal, so that the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. That match is just the statement gᵢ⋅g_j = g_j⋅gᵢ.

paragraphs.heading: Abelian groups as ℤ-modules
paragraphs.text: Abelian groups lie underneath fields, rings, vector spaces and algebras; every ring, for instance, is an abelian group under its addition. Written additively, a whole number n times an element x means x added to itself n times, and (−n)x means −(nx). This lets the integers scale the elements, which makes every abelian group a module over ℤ in exactly one way. Going the other direction, every ℤ-module is an abelian group under its addition, so the two ideas agree.

paragraphs.heading: Well understood
paragraphs.text: Abelian groups are generally easier to handle in theory than non-abelian ones, and the finite abelian groups are completely classified. A finitely generated abelian group splits into two pieces. One is built from finitely many groups ℤ/p^kℤ, with p prime, joined in a direct sum, and the other is finitely many copies of ℤ, again joined in a direct sum. Among finite abelian groups, the simple ones are just the cyclic groups whose order is a prime.
